newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Monopolies stifle trade in Bosnian Serb territory.
newsitem.headline: Monopolies stifle trade in Bosnian Serb territory.

text.p: Bosnian Serb authorities are suffocating economic growth through monopolies and strict border controls that have plunged Serb territory into severe depression, foreign experts and economists say.
Senior officials of the ruling party in Bosnia's autonomous Serb republic control trade in fuel and other profitable goods while imposing steep fees and licenses on private firms, experts say.

Members of the Serb Democratic Party (SDS) are enjoying hefty profits from the monopolies and barring entrepreneurs from trading with the country's Moslem-Croat federation or with neighbouring Croatia on Bosnia's northern border.

Western diplomats say Serb leaders have refused initiatives to allow a free flow of goods across border crossings with Croatia, a pre-war commerical route for the Banja Luka region in the western half of the Serb republic.
As a result, the Banja Luka region -- once a prosperous industrial and agricultrual centre -- is languishing in poverty and isolation 18 months after the end of the Bosnian war.
Farmers and businessmen are forced to pay higher transport costs to send goods to neighbouring Yugoslavia to the east, a less attractive market already saturated with agricultural products.
"We can't do anything until these border crossings are open," Nenad Bastinac, a member of an opposition party in Banja Luka, told Reuters.
Diplomats say two state companies, Centrex and Select-Impex, exert exclusive control over imports of fuel, cigarettes, alcohol and coffee in the Serb republic, which covers 49 percent of Bosnia.
The companies are controlled by Serb leader and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic and his ally, Momcilo Krajisnik, a member of the peacetime collective presidency.
"Opening up the border with Croatia could be economically catastrophic for some people in the government who have a monopoly and who are living well on closed borders," Bastinac said.

"It would also break the monopoly on trade with the Moslem-Croat federation enjoyed by two state companies which are run by people at the top of the government," said Bastinac, a member of the Union for Peace and Progress.
Profits worth tens of millions of dollars have paid for the loyalty of a vast police force and enriched party members.
Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic tried to blow the whistle on alleged corruption and called for an investigation into business dealings by the companies.
But Plavsic's request was ignored and her rival, Krajisnik, has since moved to undermine her authority.

By cutting off traditional trade connections and relying on the troubled economy of Yugoslavia, the Serb republic is plagued by huge arrears in social payments, rampant unemployment and feeble productivity, foreign experts say.
The average wage in Serb territory, about 67 German marks a month ($40), is a third of the average in the Moslem-Croat federation.
At least 61 percent of the work force is unemployed and the economy is operating at 20 percent of industrial capacity.
Serb leaders blame the economic crisis on the disparity in the amount of international aid donated to the federation and the Serb entity.
The Serb republic has received only about two percent of the total amount of aid for Bosnia because Serb leaders did not attend an international donors' conference last year.

Serb leaders refused to join a unified delegation representing Bosnia and wanted to attend as a separate delegation. Serb political sources said they expected $800 million in reconstruction aid for 1998.
